title: Legal and regulatory frameworks across the four UK nations
blurb: Tell statute from case law and guidance, know which regulator covers what in each UK nation, and meet midwives' mandatory reporting duties.
question: A midwife in Birmingham cares for a 16-year-old in labour and sees physical signs that female genital mutilation has been carried out. The girl says it happened in childhood. What must the midwife do?

teach.body: SPM 1.2 asks midwives to act within legal, regulatory and governance requirements, policies and ethical frameworks, including mandatory reporting duties, and to tell apart the devolved legislatures of the UK. Statute is law made by Parliament or a devolved legislature. Common law is law made by judges' decisions, such as Montgomery. Guidance, such as NICE, is not mandatory but must be taken fully into account. Professional standards, such as the NMC Code, bind you as a registrant.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives (2019) 1.2

teach.caption: Code 20.4: keep to the laws of the country in which you are practising.

head: Nation
Capacity law
System regulator
teach.caption: HIW: Healthcare Inspectorate Wales; HIS: Healthcare Improvement Scotland; RQIA: Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority. The Mental Capacity Act (NI) 2016 is only partly in force (Phase 1, 2019: deprivation of liberty, money and valuables, research).

steps.label: Discover
steps.sub: Girl under 18 discloses, or signs seen

steps.label: Notify police
steps.sub: Personally; chief officer where she lives

teach.caption: The notification does not breach confidence. For women 18 and over, assess safeguarding risk (e.g. to daughters or an unborn girl).

teach.body: Aisha, 16, is in labour in Birmingham. Her midwife, Grace, sees physical signs of FGM; Aisha says it was done when she was little. Because Aisha is under 18 and Grace is a healthcare professional working in England, s5B requires Grace to notify the police within one month of discovery. It does not matter that it happened long ago or abroad. Grace explains this sensitively to Aisha, follows safeguarding procedures and documents carefully.

items: Birth notification: notify every birth within 36 hours (NHS Act 2006 s269).
Tell the NMC and employer about any caution, charge or conviction as soon as you can (Code 23.2).
Share information to safeguard a child: in England, from 30 September 2026, s16LA Children Act 2004 creates a duty to share relevant information, and doing so does not breach confidence.
In England, trusts notify certain maternity and newborn incidents to MNSI for independent investigation.

teach.text: The FGM police-notification duty is narrow: a girl UNDER 18, a KNOWN case (disclosed or physical signs seen), in ENGLAND or WALES. A woman aged 18 or over with FGM triggers a safeguarding assessment, not a mandatory police report. And the NMC regulates you; the CQC (England) regulates your organisation.

items: Statute and common law bind; NICE guidance is not mandatory but is taken fully into account; the NMC Code binds registrants.
NMC regulates midwives UK-wide; system regulators are CQC (England), HIW (Wales), HIS (Scotland), RQIA (Northern Ireland).
Capacity law: MCA 2005 (England and Wales), AWI 2000 (Scotland), MCA (NI) 2016.
FGM s5B (England and Wales): known FGM in under-18s reported to police within one month.
Abortion Act 1967 does not extend to Northern Ireland; s16LA child information-sharing duty in force 30 Sep 2026.

summary: You can now distinguish statute, case law, guidance and professional standards, and name the regulator and capacity law in each UK nation. You can also apply midwives' mandatory reporting duties, including FGM notification and birth notification.

A.q: Which body regulates individual midwives across all four UK nations?
A.why: The NMC is the UK-wide professional regulator for nurses and midwives (and nursing associates in England).

whyNot.1: The CQC regulates providers in England, not individual midwives.
whyNot.2: The RCM is a professional body and trade union, not a regulator.
whyNot.3: HIS is the healthcare improvement and scrutiny body for Scotland, not a professional regulator.

A.q: Within what time must a midwife notify the police after discovering FGM in a girl under 18 in England?
A.why: FGM Act 2003 s5B(5)(c): before the end of one month from first discovering that FGM appears to have been carried out.

whyNot.0: 72 hours is not the statutory period.
whyNot.1: 7 days is not the statutory period.
whyNot.2: The statute says one month, not 28 days.

A.q: Which capacity legislation applies to a midwife practising in Glasgow?
A.why: Scotland has its own capacity law: the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000. Code 4.3: keep to the mental capacity law of the country where you practise.

whyNot.0: The MCA 2005 applies in England and Wales.
whyNot.1: This is Northern Ireland's capacity law (partly in force), not Scotland's.
whyNot.2: The Mental Health Act concerns mental disorder, not general capacity, and applies in England and Wales.

B.q: A midwife in Cardiff sees a 24-year-old woman at booking who has had FGM. What is the correct action?
options: Notify the police within one month
Carry out a safeguarding risk assessment
Record it; no further action is needed
B.why: The s5B police duty applies to girls under 18. For a woman of 18 or over, the midwife records it and assesses safeguarding risk, for example to daughters or an unborn girl.

whyNot.0: Mandatory police notification is for girls under 18.
whyNot.2: There is no 72-hour rule, and she is an adult.
whyNot.3: FGM must be recorded and safeguarding risk assessed, including for any daughters.

B.q: A woman moving from England to Northern Ireland asks whether the Abortion Act 1967 applies there. What is the accurate answer?
options: Yes, it applies throughout the UK
No, NI has its own framework
No, abortion is not lawful in NI
B.why: The Abortion Act 1967 extends to England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own framework under the Abortion (Northern Ireland) Regulations 2020.

whyNot.0: The Act does not extend to Northern Ireland.
whyNot.1: The Act does not apply in NI at any gestation.
whyNot.3: Abortion is lawful in NI under its own regulations.

B.q: Within how many hours must a birth be notified under the NHS Act 2006 s269?
B.why: NHS Act 2006 s269: every birth must be notified within 36 hours.

whyNot.1: 12 hours is not the statutory period.
whyNot.2: 24 hours is not the statutory period.
whyNot.3: 72 hours is the NIPE examination window, not birth notification.

C.q: A midwife in England is concerned about a woman's 2-year-old after the woman discloses heavy drug use by her partner, who looks after the child. The children's social care team asks for relevant information. The woman has not consented. What is the legal position from 30 September 2026?
options: Consent is needed before any sharing
Share it after a court order is made
Share it once a strategy meeting is held
C.why: Children Act 2004 s16LA (in force 30 Sep 2026, bodies in England under s11) creates a duty to share information relevant to safeguarding or promoting a child's welfare with other such bodies, including on request, unless disclosure would be more detrimental to the child; consent is not required and the disclosure does not breach confidence (s16LA(3), (5), (7)).

whyNot.0: Consent is not required under the new duty.
whyNot.2: The duty applies on request now; it does not wait for a strategy meeting.

C.q: A woman complains that a maternity unit in Swansea is chronically understaffed. Which organisation inspects that unit?
C.why: Healthcare Inspectorate Wales is the system regulator for healthcare services in Wales.

whyNot.0: The CQC regulates providers in England.
whyNot.1: The NMC regulates individual registrants, not services.
whyNot.3: NHS England commissions and leads the NHS in England; it does not inspect Welsh units.

C.q: A student asks why NICE guidance is described as 'not mandatory'. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Midwives can disregard it if they prefer another approach
It is advisory, so it carries no professional weight
It must be taken fully into account with the woman's needs
It applies to doctors, not to midwives
C.why: NICE guidance is not mandatory, but professionals are expected to take it fully into account, alongside the individual needs, preferences and values of the person.

whyNot.0: Departing from guidance needs a sound, documented clinical reason, not personal preference.
whyNot.1: Guidance carries significant weight; Code 6.1 requires evidence-based practice.
whyNot.3: NICE maternity guidance applies to all professionals, including midwives.

reteach.title: Ask: what, who, where?
reteach.question: Faced with a legal question, which three things do you need to know?

blocks.body: WHAT kind of rule is it: statute, case law, guidance or the Code? WHO does it bind: you as a midwife (NMC), or the organisation (CQC, HIW, HIS, RQIA)? WHERE are you: England, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland? Many maternity laws differ by nation, so always check where the care is happening.

blocks.text: FGM s5B: England and Wales, under 18, known case, police within one month.

explain.body: Statute (Acts and regulations), common law (judges' decisions), professional standards (the Code) and guidance (NICE, local policy). Guidance is not mandatory but is taken fully into account.

test.q: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board is an example of which type of law?
test.why: Montgomery is a Supreme Court judgment: common (case) law.

whyNot.0: Statute is made by Parliament or a devolved legislature.
whyNot.1: Secondary legislation is made by ministers under an Act.
whyNot.3: Guidance is issued by bodies such as NICE or the NMC.

explain.body: NMC: individual midwives, UK-wide. System regulators: CQC (England), HIW (Wales), HIS (Scotland), RQIA (Northern Ireland).

test.q: Which body is the system regulator for health services in Scotland?

explain.body: Capacity law, statutory candour, abortion law and FGM reporting differ between nations. Code 4.3 and 20.4: follow the law where you practise.

test.q: Which statement about the Abortion Act 1967 is correct?
options: It applies in all four UK nations
It does not extend to Northern Ireland
It applies in England and Wales but not Scotland
It was repealed in Scotland in 2020
test.why: The Act extends to England, Wales and Scotland; Northern Ireland has its own 2020 Regulations.

whyNot.0: It does not extend to Northern Ireland.
whyNot.3: It has not been repealed in Scotland.

explain.body: FGM in under-18s to police within a month (England and Wales). Birth notification within 36 hours. Cautions and charges to the NMC (Code 23.2). Child safeguarding information sharing (s16LA from 30 Sep 2026).

test.q: Within what period must parents register a birth in England and Wales?
test.why: Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953 s2: register within 42 days.

whyNot.0: 21 days is not the period in England and Wales.
whyNot.1: 28 days is not the statutory period.
whyNot.2: 36 hours is for birth notification by the health professional.
